segments.title: Article 8's exempt-vessel rules
segments.summary: Article 8 exempted small naval vessels, but used displacement, gun-calibre, torpedo, speed, armour, mine, and aircraft rules to stop evasions.
segments.body: Article 8 distinguishes minor combatants and fleet auxiliaries from limited warships. Vessels at or below 600 tons were exempt, while those up to 2,000 tons had to avoid features that made them too capable. The treaty covered design intent as well as fitted equipment, especially for torpedoes, speed, armour, mines, aircraft facilities, and guns above the three-inch and 6.1-inch thresholds. Those detailed exclusions created the legal space in which sloops and motor torpedo boats could exist without simply becoming uncounted cruisers.

evidence.note: The treaty text sets the 600- and 2,000-ton bands and lists the prohibited characteristics.
The speakers connect Article 8 to sloops, motor torpedo boats, and other exempt types.

segments.title: Why carriers were limited to six-inch guns
segments.summary: The six-inch limit on carrier guns closed off a loophole in which a nominal flight deck could conceal an eight-inch-gun cruiser.
segments.body: The carrier gun limit was an anti-evasion measure with consequences beyond aviation. A navy might otherwise classify a cruiser-sized warship as an aircraft carrier by adding only a token flight deck. The result could have been a heavily armed fast ship that consumed carrier rather than cruiser allowance. A deliberately exaggerated sketch combines 10,000 tons, 32.5 knots, 24 aircraft, nine six-inch guns, and eight five-inch guns. It shows why weapon limits were needed to protect the treaty's allocation system.

evidence.note: The discussion describes the risk of building a cruiser with a token flight deck and eight-inch guns.
A deliberately exaggerated carrier-cruiser hybrid illustrates the loophole being prevented.

segments.title: The six-inch threshold and small-cruiser pressure
segments.summary: Six-inch guns marked the point at which a ship became a dangerous cruiser, pressuring smaller navies not to turn destroyers into miniature cruisers.
segments.body: The treaty repeatedly returns to 6.1-inch calibre because it marked the boundary of cruiser armament. Royal Navy destroyers and sloops normally carried much smaller 4.7-inch and four-inch guns. The restriction therefore bore hardest on powers seeking maximum gun power in destroyer-sized hulls. Later interest in 5.9-inch weapons shows how designers could search for room immediately below the treaty threshold.

evidence.note: The speakers identify 6.1 inches as the cruiser boundary and contrast it with Royal Navy destroyer and sloop guns.
The transcript notes interest in 5.9-inch guns as a way of pressing against the limit.

segments.title: Treaty pressure and the super-destroyer race
segments.summary: Limits on small combatants encouraged competing destroyer philosophies, from near-cruiser gun armaments to rapid-fire destroyer weapons.
segments.body: The treaty left navies free to pursue different destroyer designs within its limits. Its pressures encouraged large destroyers, destroyer leaders, and the later Tribal class as designers balanced calibre, gun numbers, and hull size. An American example compares the short five-inch/25 with longer weapons before the Bureau of Ordnance proposes a five-inch/38. Some navies pressed toward cruiser-calibre guns, while others chose more rapid-firing weapons suited to a destroyer's actual role. Arms control redirected competition into design choices instead of ending it.

evidence.note: The discussion connects the treaty to Tribal-class and other super-destroyer design choices.
The speakers contrast proposed American destroyer guns with the five-inch/38 and its practical virtues.

segments.title: Destroyers: rapid fire, screening, and torpedoes
segments.summary: A destroyer's main anti-capital-ship weapon was the torpedo; fast-firing guns helped it screen friendly heavy ships and fight enemy destroyers.
segments.body: Destroyer gunnery followed the ship's screening role rather than a pursuit of maximum gun size. A small, fast, moving hull was poorly suited to slow long-range precision gunnery, so rate of fire and quick changes of aim mattered more. Locally controlled mounts, including hand-trained single guns, could still put shells on target quickly. At a 5 percent hit rate, 20 shells in two minutes might produce one hit while a battleship fired only four salvos. Destroyers used that gunfire to disrupt opposing destroyers and keep them from reaching capital ships with torpedoes. Their own torpedoes remained the decisive threat against larger vessels, making an over-gunned 'small cruiser' a poor substitute for a true destroyer.

evidence.note: Rapid firing is contrasted with battleship salvos and tied to fighting enemy destroyers.
The transcript identifies torpedoes as the destroyer's anti-big-ship weapon and critiques treating it as a small cruiser.

segments.title: National destroyer solutions and the six-inch cruiser
segments.summary: British, American, Japanese, French, and Italian design choices reveal different answers to torpedo armament, destroyer guns, sea conditions, and cruiser firepower.
segments.body: National destroyer designs reflected different compromises. American and Japanese large destroyers concentrated heavily on torpedoes, while the Royal Navy added more destroyer guns without losing sight of the torpedo role. French and Italian ships occupied the space between very large destroyers and very small cruisers. They suited Mediterranean conditions, though the discussion raises doubts about their behaviour in rougher seas beyond that theatre. The Royal Navy's preference for six-inch cruisers followed a related calculation: six-inch guns could fight another cruiser without the weight penalty of an eight-inch battery, leaving more displacement for protection.

evidence.note: The speakers compare British, American, Japanese, French, and Italian destroyer philosophies.
The transcript introduces the six-inch cruiser argument and the weight penalty of an eight-inch battery.

segments.title: Eight-inch turrets and firing while withdrawing
segments.summary: High-angle eight-inch mounts, faster turret traverse, and the Battle class's gun layout connect machinery choices to manoeuvre and torpedo tactics.
segments.body: Six- and eight-inch cruiser batteries imposed different weight and protection choices. An eight-inch gun could be more than was needed against another cruiser, while a six-inch battery saved weight for armour. Royal Navy eight-inch turrets also show that a lighter gun did not guarantee a lighter mounting. Early mounts could elevate to about 70 degrees and were used in the anti-aircraft role. A later Mark II gun intended to save weight ended up in a heavier turret that traversed much faster. Fast traverse mattered during hard turns or withdrawal, when slow mounts could leave the battery pointing to the wrong side. The same tactical logic shaped the Battle-class destroyers' forward gun concentration, which allowed fire over the stern while the ship withdrew after launching torpedoes.

evidence.note: The speakers contrast six- and eight-inch weight choices, the high elevation of early eight-inch mounts, and the later turret's unexpectedly greater weight but faster traverse.
Fast traverse and the Battle class's forward guns are tied to firing astern while withdrawing after a torpedo attack.

segments.title: Article 9 and controlled fleet replacement
segments.summary: Article 9 linked replacement to schedules, preventing a navy from rebuilding its whole fleet at once around the treaty's new limits.
segments.body: Article 9 governed the replacement of non-carrier warships up to 10,000 tons. It prevented a state from immediately discarding its existing fleet and replacing every ship with a design optimised for the new rules. Rival navies therefore faced less pressure to fund a sudden replacement race of their own. Reported specifications might still be misleading, but the existence and broad characteristics of a physical ship were harder to conceal.

evidence.note: Article 9's replacement rule and its scheduling purpose are discussed.
The speakers use exaggerated examples to show why fleet replacement and major ship characteristics were difficult to disguise.

segments.title: Article 10's notification and verification system
segments.summary: Article 10 required notice of a ship's laying down and completion, along with dimensions, displacement, and main-gun information that enabled outside scrutiny.
segments.body: Article 10 supplied the information-sharing machinery behind treaty enforcement. Contracting parties had to notify one another within a month of laying down or completing covered vessels. Each notice included classification, standard displacement, dimensions, draft, and largest-gun calibre. The declarations might be misleading, but naval architects could compare them with photographs and basic calculations. Transparency narrowed the room in which a navy could conceal a major discrepancy.

evidence.note: The treaty text lists the notices and technical particulars required for covered ships.
The speakers discuss naval intelligence, published reference works, and checking declarations against visible ship characteristics.

segments.title: Why treaty-era choices lasted into World War II
segments.summary: Treaty categories and replacement rules shaped ships that navies carried into World War II because there was too little time to undo every interwar design compromise.
segments.body: The discussion pauses after Article 10 to connect the treaty with warships that entered World War II. Limits on categories, weapons, and replacement schedules shaped many of the designs examined earlier in the episode. Navies did not have enough time to redesign and replace every affected ship before the war. Carrier armament, destroyer guns, and replacement timing show how interwar arms control continued to influence wartime fleets.

evidence.note: The speakers say that the treaty governed many features later seen in World War II and that there was not enough time to fix all of them.

segments.title: Counterfactual reasoning versus alternate history
segments.summary: Before proposing an earlier Pacific war, the discussion distinguishes a bounded counterfactual from an alternate-history narrative that follows one imagined path much further.
segments.body: The methodological pause defines counterfactual reasoning as a limited change followed through its immediate range of possibilities. Alternate history instead selects one imagined development and pursues it much further. That distinction frames the following 1937-38 war scenario as a test of how treaty policy could alter strategic timing. It is a way to explore possible consequences, rather than a claim that events certainly would have followed that path.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke distinguishes one-step counterfactual analysis from an alternate-history narrative before introducing his treaty scenario.

segments.title: A counterfactual early Japanese-American war
segments.summary: The closing counterfactual argues that without the London Treaty's modifications to the Washington system, Japan might have felt compelled to strike the United States in 1937 or 1938.
segments.body: The scenario asks how long the Washington system alone might have constrained the naval balance. The Imperial Japanese Navy might have feared that unrestricted American construction would pull the United States too far ahead by the late 1930s or early 1940s, encouraging a strike in 1937 or 1938. Japan's expansion in China and Fleet Problems that gathered the American fleet toward Hawaii and the central Pacific could have provided both a motive and a concentrated target. The Royal Navy might then have entered the conflict under more favourable conditions than in 1941, while Japanese assumptions of affinity with Britain as another island power went unreciprocated. This remains an explicit counterfactual about how treaty limits could shape perceptions of strategic timing, rather than a claim that an earlier war was inevitable.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke proposes that the treaty changes delayed a Pacific war by easing Japanese fears of an imminent American naval lead.
They outline a possible Japanese strike in 1937 or 1938 alongside the war in China and American fleet concentration near Hawaii.
